Tundra vole (Microtus oeconomus) neonates emerge from the uterus weighing approximately 2.9 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.9 grams] at a core body temperature of 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C], a modest birth mass that reflects the altricial nature of this arvicoline rodent. This initial wet weight is consistent with values reported for other members of the genus Microtus, where neonatal mass typically falls below three grams. The suckling juvenile grows rapidly during the first weeks of life, nourished exclusively by maternal milk until it begins the dietary transition to solid foods. Under the core body temperature typical of this species, maintained at 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C], the interval between parturition and the end of lactation, or weaning, is approximately 19 days after birth [tx = approximately 19 days after birth]. This relatively brief suckling stage is characteristic of small-bodied microtines that inhabit highly seasonal environments, where accelerated juvenile development confers a distinct advantage in terms of early independence and recruitment into the breeding population before the onset of winter conditions.

Reproduction in the tundra vole is characterized by a high intrinsic capacity for population growth, underpinned by the production of litters containing an average of seven pups. Field studies have documented that females commonly produce one litter of seven offspring per reproductive event [N_R_i = seven offspring per reproductive event] across the breeding season. Under the thermoneutral conditions of 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C], which approximates the species' active metabolic temperature, reproductive output translates into an impressive maximum rate of 3.5 litters per year [F_R_i = 3.5 litters per year], a frequency that allows rapid population turnover in ephemeral wetland habitats. This fecundity schedule enables a single female to contribute substantially to the next generation within a single summer, a life-history strategy that compensates for elevated mortality rates experienced during the long, harsh Arctic winter months. The combination of moderate litter size and high annual frequency represents a classic r-selected reproductive strategy.

Gestation in Microtus oeconomus proceeds for 22 days [tg = 22 days] when measured at the species' typical body temperature of 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C], a duration that is relatively short compared to other rodents of similar adult body size. This abbreviated gestation period is coupled with a pattern of postpartum estrus, allowing females to conceive again almost immediately after parturition, thereby maximizing the number of litters produced over the summer months. The pre-weaning juvenile phase ends when the pup reaches a wet weight at weaning of 27 grams [Wwx = 27 grams] at the same stable body temperature of 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C], signaling the transition to nutritional independence. This weaning mass is approximately two-thirds of the ultimate adult body mass attained later in life, reflecting the substantial growth that occurs during the suckling stage. The successful completion of weaning is a critical milestone, as juveniles must then forage independently to accumulate sufficient body reserves before the onset of winter hibernation.

Sexual maturation in the tundra vole exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism in timing, a pattern that has been documented in several captive breeding colonies. Female pups raised at the species' core body temperature of 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C] typically reach puberty at 30 days after birth [tp = 30 days after birth], a developmental pace that allows females born early in the season to breed within the same summer. Male pups, in contrast, attain puberty at 48 days after birth [tp = 48 days after birth], a delay that may reflect the additional time required for testicular development and the establishment of dominance hierarchies necessary for successful mating at a temperature of 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C]. This divergence in maturation rates is hypothesized to be driven by differential selection pressures: early female reproduction maximizes lifetime fecundity, whereas delayed male maturation allows for greater competitive ability during the breeding season, a trade-off observed across many polygynous rodent species.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the tundra vole, derived from comparative data on the closely related collared lemming Dicrostonyx groenlandicus, is approximately 3.3 years [am = approximately 3.3 years] when individuals are maintained at a stable body temperature of 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C]. This longevity is modest relative to that of larger arvicoline rodents but is sufficient to allow multiple breeding seasons in species that inhabit unpredictable Arctic environments. The ultimate wet weight achieved by fully grown adults is 40 grams [Wwi = 40 grams] when measured at the same species-typical temperature of 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C], a value that positions this species at the smaller end of the body size spectrum within the genus Microtus. This modest adult mass is associated with high mass-specific metabolic rates, requiring individuals to consume large quantities of herbaceous vegetation daily to sustain their energy balance. Field observations suggest that senescence typically manifests as a decline in body condition and reproductive output during the third year of life.
